newsitem.title: USA: Albright stresses importance of a Chile trade pact.
newsitem.headline: Albright stresses importance of a Chile trade pact.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Wednesday stressed the importance of concluding a comprehensive trade agreement with Chile and hailed bilateral ties between Washington and Santiago.

At the start of talks with Chile's foreign minister, she said they would discuss many issues, including President Bill Clinton's request for special authority "for the purpose of securing a comprehensive trade agreement with Chile and of moving ahead on our overall global trade agenda."

U.S. officials said Albright and Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza were also expected to discuss Chile's interest in purchasing advanced fighter jets, including F-16s from American producers Lockheed and McDonnell Douglas.

Answering questions at a brief joint news conference, Albright did not make a public pitch for the U.S. firms. "It is obviously up to Chile to decide what it wishes to do in modernizing its air force," she said.

Clinton last week said one of his priorities for 1997 was getting Congress to give his administration so-called fast-track negotiating authority for trade agreements. If it did, Congress would be able to approve or reject the accords but not amend them.

The White House wants the authority most immediately to negotiate a trade agreement with Chile, which already has separate pacts with Canada and Mexico, the United States' partners in the North American Free Trade Agreeemnt.

But it hopes to expand NAFTA into a free trade pact covering all of North and South America, pursue separate trade negotiations with Asian-Pacific nations and conduct further global negotiations under the World Trade Organization.

U.S. officials have acknowledged that Clinton faces a major challenge in obtaining fast-track authority, because many congressmen question the need for additional trade pacts despite the importance of exports to the U.S. economy.

On Aug. 6 Richard Brown, U.S. senior coordinator of the Summit of the Americas, said in Buenos Aires that the United States was leaning toward a bilateral trade pact with Chile rather than seeking its full entry into NAFTA, in part because Santiago had already negotiated separate free trade pacts with Mexico and Canada.
Clinton is to visit Chile for the second Summit of the Americas, scheduled for April 1998 in Santiago.
On Aug. 1, in a major boost for Latin America and U.S. arms dealers, Clinton ended a 20-year-old ban on the sale of high-tech weaponry to Latin America.

Analysts say the resumption of sales from U.S. manufacturers was inevitable once Peru went shopping in Eastern Europe and Chile started looking at Western European planes in the event they could not buy the U.S. F-16s they really want. U.S. arms makers have been desperate for new markets since the end of the Cold War.
U.S. critics of Clinton's decision to lift the ban fear it will trigger an arms race in Latin America and undermine attempts of countries there to strengthen their incipient democracies.
But regional officials say that while the decision is likely to increase military spending, it should not trigger an arms race.
Albright stressed on Wednesday that under the new policy, each country's request for high-tech weaponry would be decided individually.
Insulza, at the news conference, objected that the spotlight was on Chile when the new sales policy affected the entire region.
